summary: This standards-track document defines CBOR Web Token, a compact way to represent claims transferred between two parties. The claims are encoded in CBOR and protected with COSE for application-layer security. It is like JWT, but suited to constrained environments.

plainLanguage.summary: A small, signed note that says things about you, like a mini ID card. It is written compactly so little gadgets can carry it.

subtitle: JWT's compact cousin: signed or encrypted claims encoded in CBOR instead of JSON, for small devices.

tldr.problem: JSON Web Tokens are popular, but JSON is considered inefficient for some Internet of Things systems that use low-power radio technologies.
tldr.mechanism: A CWT carries the same kind of claims as a JWT, but as a CBOR map with integer keys, and protects them with COSE signing, MAC or encryption.
tldr.outcome: It gives constrained systems a compact, JWT-derived token format with a claims registry, a media type (application/cwt) and an optional CBOR tag (61).

today: RFC 8392 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the CWT format and the IANA registries for CWT claims.

sections.title: Why a CBOR Version of JWT
sections.content:
The JSON Web Token (JWT, RFC 7519) is a standard security token format used in OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect deployments, among other things. It secures a set of claims written in JSON using JSON Web Signature and JSON Web Encryption. JSON suits Web and native applications, but the RFC says it is considered inefficient for some Internet of Things systems that use low-power radio technologies.

RFC 8392 defines the CBOR Web Token (CWT): the same idea, but with claims encoded in CBOR (RFC 7049) and protected with COSE (RFC 8152). The name and pronunciation come from JWT; the suggested pronunciation is the English word "cot".

A claim is a piece of information asserted about a subject, written as a name and value pair.
sections.plainLanguage: A JWT is a note written in long, wordy language. A CWT says the same things in a short code, so it fits on tiny devices that cannot carry much.

sections.title: Claims and Their Integer Keys
sections.content:
A CWT carries a CWT Claims Set: a CBOR map holding the claims. The Claim Name is the human-readable label, the Claim Key is the CBOR map key and the Claim Value is the value. JSON objects only allow string keys. CBOR also allows integers, which the RFC says gives compactness of encoding and easy comparison.

The seven registered claims mirror JWT: iss (issuer), sub (subject), aud (audience), exp (expiration time), nbf (not before), iat (issued at) and cti (CWT ID, the counterpart of the JWT jti claim). None are mandatory. Applications decide which claims they use and when they are required, and a recipient MUST ignore claims it does not understand unless the application says otherwise.

Times use a NumericDate encoded as a CBOR numeric date with the leading tag 1 omitted. Claim values MUST NOT be prefixed with CBOR tags, since that would only take up space.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of writing "issuer" on a label, the note just uses the number 1. Everybody agrees on what the numbers mean, so the note stays tiny.

sections.title: CWT Wire Format and the CWT Tag
sections.content:
A CWT is a COSE object (signed, MACed or encrypted) whose payload is the claims set. COSE then does the cryptographic work, using COSE_Sign/COSE_Sign1, COSE_Mac/COSE_Mac0 or COSE_Encrypt/COSE_Encrypt0.

How a receiver knows that a CBOR object is a CWT is application dependent. It may be clear from context, or a transport can use the application/cwt content type. The RFC also defines an optional CWT CBOR tag, 61, for cases where this would not otherwise be known. If present, it MUST prefix a tagged object that uses one of the COSE CBOR tags, as in 61(17(...)) for a COSE_Mac0.
sections.plainLanguage: The note is sealed in a COSE envelope. You can stick a label on the envelope that says "this is a CWT", but only if the people reading it would not already know.

sections.title: Creating and Validating a CWT
sections.content:
To create a CWT, you build the claims set, take its binary form as the Message, make a COSE header, and wrap the Message in a signed, MACed or encrypted COSE object, following all the steps in RFC 8152. For nesting, you can wrap the result again. Finally you may prepend the COSE tag and the CWT tag if the application needs them.

To validate, a receiver checks that the data is valid CBOR, strips the CWT tag if present, finds the COSE type from the tag or from application context, and checks that the COSE header contains only parameters it understands or that can be ignored. It then verifies the signature or MAC, or decrypts. If the result starts with a COSE tag it is a nested CWT and the process repeats. At the end the Message must be a valid CBOR map, which is the claims set. If any step fails, the CWT MUST be rejected.
sections.plainLanguage: To make one, you write the note, then seal it. To check one, you open the seals one by one and make sure each is real. If any seal looks fake, you throw the whole thing away.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A CWT is only as secure as the COSE protection on it. Unless the claims are protected, an adversary can modify, add or remove claims. Because claims may drive authorization decisions, the recipient must also be able to authenticate the party that created the CWT, and the creator needs to evaluate each claim value carefully before including it.

For nested CWTs, the RFC says that when both signing and encryption are needed, producers normally should sign first and then encrypt the result. That prevents attacks where the signature is stripped, leaving just an encrypted message, and it provides privacy for the signer.
sections.plainLanguage: If the note is not locked or signed, anyone can scribble on it. If you need both a signature and a secret, sign first and then lock it in the box, not the other way round.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA created a CBOR Web Token (CWT) Claims registry. Key ranges use different policies: integers from -256 to 255 and one-character strings are Standards Action, integers from -65536 to -257 and from 256 to 65535 and two-character strings are Specification Required, larger values and longer strings are Expert Review, and integers below -65536 are Private Use. Key 0 is reserved.

The RFC also registers the application/cwt media type, CoAP Content-Format ID 61 for it, and CBOR tag 61 for CWT.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a public sign-up sheet for claim numbers. Small numbers are scarce and need serious reasons, while big numbers are easy to get.

sections.title: Appendix Examples
sections.content: Appendix A shows one claims set that uses every defined claim, then protects it several ways: signed, MACed, encrypted, nested signing and encryption, and a MACed CWT with a floating-point value. It uses 128-bit and 256-bit symmetric keys and an ECDSA P-256 key, and presents each as a hex string and in CBOR diagnostic notation.
sections.plainLanguage: The back of the book has worked examples, so you can check your own sealed notes against the right answers.

data.title: Example claims set
data.code:
{
  / iss / 1: "coap://as.example.com",
  / sub / 2: "erikw",
  / aud / 3: "coap://light.example.com",
  / exp / 4: 1444064944,
  / nbf / 5: 1443944944,
  / iat / 6: 1443944944,
  / cti / 7: h'0b71'
}
